definition: Capital-B Bitcoin is the system: protocol, peer-to-peer network, and software. Small-b bitcoin is the unit of currency stored and transmitted on that network.
The set of rules and message formats used by peers to communicate, primarily over the internet; available as open source software that runs on laptops and smartphones.
A distributed network with no central server or point of control in which every full node (peer) connects to several others to propagate transactions and blocks.
Design property that Bitcoin has no central authority, server, or issuer; mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank.
The public transaction journal: a chain of validated blocks, each committing to its predecessor, back to the genesis block. It is the authoritative record of all confirmed transactions.
The rules every full node independently applies to validate transactions and blocks and to enforce currency issuance; miners earn rewards only for blocks that follow them.

Bitcoin's mechanism for global decentralized consensus: miners repeatedly hash candidate blocks until the hash matches a protocol template. The winning block is costly to produce but trivial to verify, so it proves work was done.

Repeatedly performing the proof-of-work computation over a candidate block of recent transactions; on average one miner succeeds every 10 minutes and is rewarded with new bitcoins plus transaction fees.
Any network participant who builds candidate blocks and searches for a valid proof of work; miners may operate alone or in pools.
A network-wide parameter that scales how hard the proof-of-work puzzle is; it is adjusted dynamically so blocks arrive every 10 minutes on average regardless of total hashing power.
The average time between blocks targeted by the protocol; individual intervals vary, the difficulty adjustment keeps the average near 10 minutes.
The fixed upper bound on bitcoins that will ever exist (slightly below 21,000,000), enforced by the issuance schedule in the consensus rules; about 99% will have been issued by around 2035.
The scheduled reduction of new-coin issuance: half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years because the block subsidy is cut in half periodically.
Because Bitcoin's issuance diminishes toward a fixed cap, the book describes the currency as deflationary over the long term.

The book's list of what Bitcoin consists of: a decentralized P2P network (the protocol), a public transaction journal (the blockchain), consensus rules for independent validation and issuance, and the proof-of-work consensus mechanism.

The risk that the same unit of digital money is spent twice. Physical cash avoids it trivially; earlier digital currencies used a central clearinghouse; Bitcoin solves it with proof-of-work consensus on a single transaction history.
A trusted central authority that settles all transactions and holds a global view of the currency, as used by banks and pre-Bitcoin digital currencies; a single point of attack that Bitcoin removes.

A cryptographic value produced with a private key over a message (transaction) that anyone can verify with the corresponding public key; proves ownership/authorization without revealing the private key.

Pseudonymous author of the 2008 paper 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' and of the 2009 reference implementation; withdrew from public view in April 2011; identity unknown; exerts no control over Bitcoin.

Nakamoto's 2008 paper describing Bitcoin: electronic coin as a chain of digital signatures, a P2P timestamp server, hash-based proof of work, longest-chain rule, incentives, SPV, and privacy via fresh key pairs. Reproduced as Appendix A of the book.
Adam Back's proof-of-work scheme that Nakamoto combined with digital signatures to build Bitcoin.

The distributed-computing problem of getting leaderless participants to agree on a course of action over an unreliable, possibly compromised network; Bitcoin's PoW consensus is a practical solution without a trusted authority.
The most common user interface to Bitcoin (like a browser is to HTTP): software that manages keys, builds and signs transactions, and tracks balances. The 'wallet database' holds keys, not coins.
The reference implementation of the Bitcoin protocol, derived from Satoshi's original client; includes a wallet, validation engine, block construction tools, and P2P networking.
Wallet running on a general-purpose OS (Windows/macOS); the first wallet type (the reference implementation); offers autonomy but inherits desktop security weaknesses.
The most common wallet type, running on iOS/Android; often simplest for new users; most fetch data from remote servers, which reduces privacy.
Wallet accessed through a browser and stored on a third-party server (like webmail); most take control of the user's keys in exchange for convenience, so large balances should not be kept there.

Special-purpose hardware that stores private keys and signs transactions (via USB, NFC, or QR codes); often called a 'hardware wallet' but must be paired with a full-featured wallet application to send and receive.

A program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions against every consensus rule; may store and serve data to others; the peers of the P2P network; offers complete autonomy at substantial resource cost.

A simplified-payment-verification client that connects to full nodes for transaction data, stores its wallet locally, partially validates what it receives, and builds its own transactions; its security depends on the integrity of its peers.
A client that interacts with Bitcoin only through a third party's API rather than the network; trusts that provider for accurate data and privacy.
Full nodes are peers that independently validate everything; lightweight wallets and other software are clients that depend on one or more peers for valid data.

Custodial: a third party controls the private keys (an account with a custodian). Noncustodial: the user controls the keys and bears backup responsibility. 'Your keys, your coins. Not your keys, not your coins.'
A wallet in which the user alone controls the private keys; the user must back up the recovery code because losing the keys loses the funds.

Numbers, letters, or words randomly selected by the wallet software that serve as the basis for all of the wallet's keys; used to rebuild the wallet after loss. Also called mnemonic, mnemonic phrase, or seed phrase.
Alternative names for a recovery code. 'Mnemonic' implies memorizing, but the book recommends writing it down; 'seed phrase' because it seeds the key-generation function.
Payments or protocols (e.g., Lightning) in which not every payment is recorded on the public blockchain; cheaper and more private, but seed-based recovery cannot guarantee restoring such funds.

A string derived from a key (or script) that directs payments to a wallet; generated independently by the wallet and never registered with any service; safe to share, but reuse links payments and harms privacy.
Receiving multiple payments to the same address; lets observers link those payments and see amounts; the book recommends a fresh address per payment request.
A payment request shared with a payer; in BIP21 form it is a QR-encoded URI containing an address, amount, label, and description so the wallet can prefill the payment.
Two-dimensional barcode used to share addresses and invoices between wallets by camera scan; bech32 addresses in uppercase use a smaller QR mode.
Bitcoin transactions cannot be reversed once confirmed, unlike credit-card, PayPal, or bank transfers; this is why sellers of bitcoin require KYC before accepting reversible payments.
A machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoins to a smartphone wallet; one of the book's listed ways for a new user to acquire bitcoin.
A market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin for local currency, usually linked to a bank account and subject to identity regulations; price is set by supply and demand.
Identity-verification requirements imposed where Bitcoin touches regulated systems such as exchanges; once an address is tied to an identity, associated transactions can be tracked.
Bitcoin's price is set by markets through supply and demand, differs slightly per market, and changes many times per second; pricing services publish a volume-weighted average (e.g., BTC/USD).
The smallest unit of bitcoin recorded on the blockchain: 0.00000001 BTC (1 BTC = 100,000,000 sats). Serialized transactions encode values as integers of this base unit.
One thousandth of a bitcoin (0.001 BTC = 100,000 satoshis); Alice's first purchase from Joe was 1 mBTC.
The implied difference between a transaction's total inputs and total outputs, collected by the miner who includes the transaction; a higher fee rate generally means faster confirmation.

Inclusion of a transaction in a block on the blockchain (one confirmation); each subsequent block adds another. 'Unconfirmed' means propagated but not yet in a block. Bitcoin's equivalent of clearing.
The traditional-finance term for a payment being finalized; in Bitcoin, confirmation of a transaction by inclusion in a block plays this role.

Bitcoin itself requires no personal information, but addresses are public: reuse, block-explorer lookups, remote-server wallets, and exchange KYC can all link activity to a person. Best practice: new address per payment.

A web application that acts as a search engine for the blockchain (addresses, transactions, blocks), e.g., Blockstream Explorer, Mempool.Space, BlockCypher; looking up your own transactions reveals your interest to the operator.
The 'bitcoin:' URI scheme for invoices: bitcoin:<address>?amount=...&label=...&message=..., usually shown as a QR code.
A signed data structure by which the owner of some bitcoins authorizes transferring that value to a new owner; each new owner can spend by creating another transaction, forming a chain of ownership.

A reference to a previous transaction output being spent (its txid plus output index) together with the proof of ownership (signature/input script). Inputs do not store their value; it is looked up from the referenced output.
A component of a transaction that receives funds: a value plus an output script that encumbers the value with spending conditions (e.g., a signature from the recipient's key).
A transaction output that has not yet been spent by any input; the set of all UTXOs is what a full node tracks and what wallets select from when building payments.

The book's description of transactions as ledger lines with inputs (debits/spending) on one side and outputs (credits/receiving) on the other, with outputs summing to slightly less than inputs (the fee).
The linkage created when the output of one transaction becomes the input of the next (e.g., Joe -> Alice -> Bob -> Gopesh), tracing ownership back through history.

The 32-byte identifier of a transaction used by inputs to reference the transaction whose output they spend (e.g., 'Tx1:0' = output 0 of Tx1). Not authoritative until confirmed because of malleability.

An output that returns excess input value to the spender because inputs cannot be partially spent; at the protocol level identical to a payment output; for privacy it usually pays a fresh address from the spender's wallet.
A transaction with a single output and no change, practical only when the input amount roughly equals the payment plus fee.
A wallet's strategy for choosing which UTXOs to spend (aggregate many small ones vs use one large one), balancing fees, change, and privacy like a person choosing bills and coins.
The most common transaction form: one input and two outputs (payment plus change).
A transaction spending several inputs into a single output, like exchanging a pile of coins for one large note; used to clean up many small amounts.
A single transaction paying many recipients through multiple outputs, e.g., payroll.
The condition placed on an output's value by its script, e.g., 'paid to whoever can present a signature from the key matching Bob's address'; the recipient's wallet satisfies it when spending.
A wallet that already knows its UTXOs can build and sign a transaction with no network connection, then broadcast it later, like writing a check at home and mailing it.

The book's fuller name for a full node: a peer with both the software logic and the data to fully verify new transactions and blocks; nodes are the dots and connections the edges in the network graph.
The propagation technique in which any node that receives a valid, previously unseen transaction (or block) forwards it to all its connected peers, reaching most of the network within seconds.
A bundle of transactions plus a small header that commits to the previous block and must satisfy proof of work; enormous computation to produce, trivial to verify.
A miner's proposed block, its 'lottery ticket', containing the transactions it wants to mine plus header fields; the miner varies it and hashes it until the hash matches the protocol's template.

A function that scrambles input data into a fixed-size output: the same input always yields the same output, but the output for a new or slightly changed input is unpredictable, and finding another input with the same output is impractical.
New bitcoins created in each block, paid together with the block's transaction fees to the miner's own address via a special transaction; the subsidy follows a fixed, diminishing schedule.

The special first transaction of a block, created by the miner, that pays the block reward plus fees to an address of the miner's choosing (the book describes it in ch02 without naming it; the whitepaper calls it the first transaction that 'starts a new coin').
A group of miners whose candidate blocks assign the reward to a pool address; the pool shares rewards with members in proportion to the work they contributed.
Fee per unit of transaction size; miners prioritize transactions with the highest fee rates when filling candidate blocks.
When competing valid chains exist, full nodes choose the one with the most total proof of work; the whitepaper phrased this as the 'longest chain'.
Nakamoto's rule that nodes consider the longest proof-of-work chain correct and keep extending it; it embodies the majority of CPU power ('one-CPU-one-vote').
The conventional depth after which a transaction is considered very hard to change, because an attacker would need to redo six blocks plus one more.
Block #0, the first block in the blockchain, to which every later block ultimately links.
A block's position in the chain, i.e., how many blocks precede it (the genesis block is height 0).

Lightweight verification that a transaction is in the blockchain by checking block headers and inclusion (Merkle branch) plus the number of blocks mined after it, without validating the whole history.
Nakamoto's conceptual building block: hash a block of items and widely publish the hash, each timestamp including the previous one, forming a chain that proves data existed at that time.
The header field a miner increments so that the block's hash meets the required difficulty (leading zero bits in the whitepaper's description).
A tree of hashes over a block's transactions whose root is committed in the block header, allowing old transactions to be pruned and SPV clients to verify inclusion with a short branch.
The implementation that provides a reference for how each part of the technology should be implemented; for Bitcoin this is Bitcoin Core, evolved from Satoshi's original 'Bitcoin' client.
Bitcoin's source code is released under the open MIT license, free to download and use for any purpose, and developed by an open community of volunteers (over 1,000 contributors by 2023).
Numbered design documents that have specified most major parts of Bitcoin since 2011 (e.g., BIP9 for upgrade deployment, BIP16 P2SH, BIP21 URIs, BIP32/39/44 wallets, BIP173/350 addresses).
The Bitcoin Core daemon (server) that runs the full node; started in the foreground with -printtoconsole or in the background with -daemon.
The command-line helper that sends JSON-RPC calls to a running bitcoind (e.g., bitcoin-cli getblockchaininfo); 'help' lists commands and 'help <cmd>' documents one.
Git tags mark Bitcoin Core versions; tags with the 'rc' suffix are release candidates for testing, stable releases have no suffix; checking out a tag leaves Git in 'detached HEAD'.

term: Build pipeline (autogen.sh, configure, make, make check, make install)
definition: Steps to compile Bitcoin Core from source: autogen.sh generates build scripts, configure detects libraries and options (e.g., --with-gui=no, --disable-wallet, --prefix=$HOME), make compiles, make check runs unit tests, make install copies bitcoind/bitcoin-cli/bitcoin-tx to /usr/local/bin.
Default location (datadir option) for the blockchain database, bitcoin.conf, the .cookie RPC password, and wallets; can use from ~10 GB (pruned) to ~1 TB.
Bitcoin Core's configuration file, read at every start; holds options such as txindex, prune, dbcache, blocksonly, maxmempool, alertnotify, datadir (more than 100 options exist).
Configuration option that builds an index of all transactions so any transaction can be fetched by txid with getrawtransaction; by default Core indexes only wallet-related transactions.
Configuration option that caps blockchain disk usage by deleting old blocks; the node still downloads and validates the entire chain.
Size of the UTXO cache in memory (default 450 MiB); larger on high-end hardware, smaller on constrained nodes.
Configuration option that minimizes bandwidth by accepting only blocks of confirmed transactions and not relaying unconfirmed transactions.
Configuration option limiting the memory used by the transaction memory pool.
A node's pool of validated but unconfirmed transactions awaiting inclusion in a block; inspected with getmempoolinfo and bounded by maxmempool.

The multi-hour or multi-day process in which a new node first fetches block headers from peers to find the chain with the most proof of work, then downloads and validates full blocks; the node cannot process transactions or show balances until done.
Bitcoin Core's API: remote procedure calls encoded as JSON over HTTP (default port 8332 on localhost), used by bitcoin-cli, curl, and wrapper libraries such as python-bitcoinlib.

Bitcoin Core writes a random RPC password to the .cookie file in its data directory at every start; bitcoin-cli reads it automatically and curl users can copy it; a static password can be made with rpcauth.py.

The most important Bitcoin Core status commands; getblockchaininfo reports chain, blocks, headers, bestblockhash, difficulty, verificationprogress, pruned; getnetworkinfo reports version, protocol, connections.

getrawtransaction <txid> returns a transaction serialized as hex (requires txindex for arbitrary transactions); decoderawtransaction <hex> decodes it into JSON showing vin, vout, scripts, addresses, and output types.

getblockhash <height> returns a block's header hash; getblock <hash> returns the block's JSON including confirmations (depth), height, merkleroot, time, mediantime, nonce, bits, difficulty, chainwork, and the tx list.
In getblock output, the number of blocks built on top of a block, indicating how hard its transactions are to change; distinct from height (blocks before it).
The median timestamp of the 11 blocks preceding a block, a time measurement harder for miners to manipulate than the block's own time field.
The ability to modify a transaction before it is confirmed in a way that changes its txid; hence a txid is not authoritative until confirmed. Segwit (2017) prevents third parties from changing txids.
Replacement of one or more recent blocks by a competing chain with more proof of work; can change a confirmed transaction's status; rare after several confirmations.
A language library that wraps Bitcoin Core's JSON-RPC API for convenience, e.g., python-bitcoinlib (not part of Bitcoin Core).
Other clients and libraries by language: bcoin, Bitcore, BitcoinJS (JavaScript); bitcoinj (Java); python-bitcoinlib, pycoin (Python); btcd (Go); rust-bitcoin (Rust); bitcoin-s (Scala); NBitcoin (C#).
The book's example that thousands of people run full nodes even on a $35 Raspberry Pi, despite the >500 GB initial download and ~400 MB/day growth (2023 figures).
A free satellite data feed that can deliver blockchain data to nodes with limited or metered internet connections.

Cryptography with a key pair: a private key that signs and a public key that verifies, built on functions easy in one direction and infeasible in reverse. In Bitcoin it provides digital signatures, not encryption.

A secret number picked at random (256 bits, 64 hex digits, in the range 0 to n-1 where n is the curve order); controls all funds of its public key; must be kept secret and backed up because a lost key means lost funds.
A point K = (x, y) on the secp256k1 curve computed as K = k x G from the private key; used to receive funds and verify signatures; cannot be reversed to the private key.
Entropy is the secure randomness needed to pick a private key; software uses a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (never a simple language RNG) to produce 256 bits.
Asymmetric cryptography based on the discrete logarithm problem over points of an elliptic curve; Bitcoin uses elliptic-curve addition and multiplication over the secp256k1 curve.

The specific elliptic curve and constants Bitcoin uses, defined by y^2 = x^3 + 7 over the finite field of prime order p; standardized (the book cites NIST); most implementations use the libsecp256k1 library.
Arithmetic modulo a very large prime p; because secp256k1 is defined over F_p rather than the reals, the curve looks like scattered points, but the geometric rules are the same.
The fixed base point of secp256k1, identical for all Bitcoin users, that is multiplied by the private key to produce the public key (K = k x G).
Adding a point to itself k times (kP); a trap-door/one-way function: easy to compute K from k, infeasible to compute k from K.
The identity element ('zero') of elliptic-curve addition; the result when the line through two points is vertical.
Finding k given K = kG; as hard as brute-force search, which is why a public key does not reveal its private key.
A function easy to compute forward and infeasible to invert (e.g., elliptic-curve multiplication); the basis for unforgeable digital signatures.

The field in a transaction output that sets the conditions for spending it (acts like a public key); e.g., P2PKH's OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG. Called 'locking script' or scriptPubKey elsewhere.
The field in a transaction input that satisfies the output script being spent (acts like a signature), e.g., <signature> <public key> for P2PKH. Called 'unlocking script' or scriptSig elsewhere.

Scripts are evaluated by pushing data items onto a stack and letting opcodes consume the top items; the input script runs first, then the output script; the script passes if a nonzero item remains on top.
An operation code in Bitcoin Script that consumes and produces stack items, e.g., OP_DUP (duplicate), OP_HASH160 (hash), OP_EQUALVERIFY (compare or fail), OP_CHECKSIG (verify signature), OP_EQUAL.
Opcode that pops a public key and a signature, verifies the signature is valid for that key and commits to the transaction, and pushes 1 on success or 0 on failure.
The original output type: <public key> OP_CHECKSIG, spent with an input script containing only a signature; used with Bitcoin 0.1's IP-address payments; never widely used.

Bitcoin 0.1 feature: the spender entered the receiver's IP address, the nodes connected, and the receiver's wallet supplied a fresh public key; removed because receivers had to be online and reachable (firewalls, NAT).
The output of a secure hash function used as a promise to its input: only that input produces that output, so a party can commit to data (e.g., a public key or script) and reveal it later.
The 256-bit (32-byte) secure hash function most commonly used in Bitcoin, for commitments, checksums (double SHA256), proof of work, and key derivation.
A 160-bit (20-byte) hash function, slightly less secure than SHA256, applied after SHA256 in legacy commitments to shorten them.
RIPEMD160(SHA256(x)): the 20-byte double hash used for P2PKH public-key commitments, P2SH redeem-script commitments, and P2WPKH witness programs.

Legacy output type paying a 20-byte HASH160 commitment to a public key: output script OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG, spent with <sig> <pubkey>; base58check addresses start with '1'.
An encoding alphabet like base64 but without the easily confused characters 0 (zero), O (capital o), l (lower L), I (capital i) and the symbols + and /; 58 symbols total.

Base58 encoding of a version byte + payload + 4-byte checksum (first 4 bytes of SHA256(SHA256(version||payload))); wallets reject mistyped strings, preventing funds sent to wrong addresses. Used for legacy addresses, WIF keys, xpub/xprv.

The byte prepended before base58check encoding that identifies the data type and determines the leading character: 0x00 P2PKH ('1'), 0x05 P2SH ('3'), 0x6F testnet P2PKH ('m'/'n'), 0xC4 testnet P2SH ('2'), 0x80 WIF private key ('5', 'K', 'L'), 0x0488B21E xpub.
Redundant data appended to detect transcription errors: 4 bytes of double SHA256 in base58check; 6 characters of a BCH code in bech32/bech32m (which can also locate errors).
The original 65-byte public key encoding: prefix 04 followed by the 32-byte x and 32-byte y coordinates (130 hex characters).

A 33-byte public key encoding storing only x plus a prefix indicating y's parity (02 if y is even, 03 if odd); backward compatible, now the default, and required for newer features. It hashes to a different address than the uncompressed form of the same key.

Output type introduced by BIP16 in 2012: the output script OP_HASH160 <20-byte hash> OP_EQUAL commits to a redeem script; the spender later supplies the redeem script plus signatures. Addresses start with '3'. Not necessarily multisig.
The full script (e.g., a 2-of-2 multisig) whose HASH160 is committed in a P2SH output; revealed in the input script at spend time and then executed.
A script requiring more than one signature to spend (e.g., desktop wallet plus hardware signer); the most common use of P2SH, though P2SH can wrap other scripts.
P2PKH ('1...') and P2SH ('3...') addresses, the only two script templates encoded with base58check; now less common, supplanted by bech32.

When an attacker can influence part of the input to a 160-bit hash (e.g., choosing their key last in a multisig), collision resistance drops to 2^80, which is within reach of large-scale hashing; newer address types give at least 128 bits, so new wallets should prefer them.
The 2017 protocol upgrade that prevents transaction IDs from being changed without the spender's consent, adds block capacity, and introduced new output types (P2WPKH, P2WSH) with bech32 addresses.

Segwit address format (BIP173): human-readable part + '1' + data in a 32-character single-case alphabet + 6-character BCH checksum; detects any error of up to 4 characters, can locate errors, encodes efficiently in QR codes, and lets wallets pay future segwit versions. 'bech' = BCH.

Bech32 with one checksum constant changed (BIP350) to fix the insertion/deletion weakness (the 'q' before a final 'p' bug); used for segwit v1 (taproot) and later; differs from bech32 only in the last six characters.
The prefix of a bech32/bech32m address identifying the network: 'bc' for Bitcoin mainnet, 'tb' for testnet; followed by the separator '1'.
The character between the HRP and data part of a bech32 address; chosen as a digit so double-click selection works, and '1' because it is not otherwise in the alphabet (avoids confusion with 'l').
The first data character of a bech32(m) address, encoding the segwit version 0-16: 'q' = version 0 (bech32, bc1q...), 'p' = version 1 taproot (bech32m, bc1p...).

The payload of a segwit output (2 to 40 bytes): for version 0 it must be 20 bytes (P2WPKH, HASH160 of a pubkey) or 32 bytes (P2WSH, SHA256 of a script); for version 1 it is a 32-byte x-only public key.
Pay to witness public key hash: segwit v0 output OP_0 <20-byte HASH160(pubkey)>; bech32 address of 42 characters starting bc1q.

Pay to witness script hash: segwit v0 output OP_0 <32-byte SHA256(script)>; uses SHA256 only (no RIPEMD-160), giving 256-bit commitments that avoid the P2SH collision weakness; 62-character bc1q address.
Segwit version 1 output OP_1 <32-byte point>, where the witness program is a public key that usually commits to additional data; addresses use bech32m and start with bc1p.
Base58check encoding of a private key with version byte 0x80, producing strings starting with '5'; used to import/export single keys between wallets and in QR codes.

WIF with a 0x01 suffix appended before encoding, producing strings starting with 'K' or 'L'; signals that only compressed public keys should be derived. 'Compressed private key' is a misnomer: the key is not compressed and the encoding is one byte longer.

A valid address containing a chosen human-readable pattern (e.g., 1Kids...), found by brute-force trial of random keys; no more or less secure than other addresses; each extra character multiplies the search by 58; largely abandoned because deterministic wallets can't import them and reuse hurts privacy.
A service where people with fast hardware search for vanity address patterns for a fee.

Private keys (often with addresses) printed on paper; the book calls them obsolete and dangerous (back-doored generators have stolen funds) and says to use recovery codes and hardware signing devices instead.
What people commonly call 'the wallet': the store of keys (public and/or private) and metadata; it contains keys, not bitcoins, which are records on the blockchain.
Early wallet design generating each key independently at random; required a new backup every time keys were generated, or funds received to un-backed-up keys were lost.
A wallet that derives all keys from a single random seed using a repeatable algorithm (e.g., hashing seed+index), so one backup of the seed covers every key ever generated.
A random value (128-512 bits; 512 bits from BIP39) from which a deterministic wallet derives all keys; whoever has the seed can derive every private key.
related: Master private key / master chain code

definition: A value added to a public key (t x G) and correspondingly to the private key (k + t) so that a child key pair can be derived; because K + tG == (k + t)G, child public keys can be derived from public information alone.
Deriving child public keys from a parent public key without any private key, using deterministic tweaks; enables wallet frontends that hand out addresses while private keys stay on a signer.

Hierarchical deterministic wallet: a tree of keys derived from one seed in which any key can be the parent of a sequence of children, with no depth limit; used by every modern wallet by default. Defined in BIP32.
The standard defining hierarchical deterministic key derivation: master key and chain code from a seed via HMAC-SHA512, normal and hardened child derivation, extended keys (xprv/xpub).

The most popular recovery-code standard (proposed by the Trezor company): 128-256 bits of entropy plus a checksum, split into 11-bit groups mapped to a 2,048-word list (12-24 words); the words plus an optional passphrase are stretched with PBKDF2 into a 512-bit seed.
BIP39's dictionary of 2,048 words (2^11), one per 11-bit segment of entropy+checksum; may be localized, but backup and recovery software must use the same list.
The Electrum wallet's word-based code: no dependency on a global word list, includes a version number, supports an optional passphrase (called a 'seed extension'), same key-stretching as BIP39.

The LND wallet's recovery code: two version numbers, a wallet birthday (creation date, so restores need not scan the whole chain), an authenticated passphrase (wrong passphrase gives an error), and stronger scrypt stretching (32,768 rounds).
The wallet's creation date embedded in an Aezeed recovery code so that restoration can skip scanning blocks from before the wallet existed.
A nonword code used by the Muun wallet that, together with an emergency-kit PDF, decrypts the wallet's private keys rather than encoding a seed; supports Lightning, descriptors, and miniscript.
A BIP39 successor that splits one seed into multiple recovery codes with a threshold (e.g., any 3 of 5 recover the seed); optional passphrase, global word list, no versioning.
A newer proposal similar to SLIP39 whose recovery-code shares (up to 31, with a threshold) can be created and verified by hand with paper tools or by software.

An optional user-chosen string appended to the salt ('mnemonic' + passphrase) when stretching the recovery code; every passphrase yields a different, valid seed ('no wrong passphrase'), giving a second factor and plausible deniability but no error detection and a risk of permanent loss.

Because any BIP39 passphrase opens a valid wallet, a user can keep a decoy wallet with a small balance behind one passphrase while the main funds sit behind another; the downside is an attacker can never be sure everything was revealed.
Keys derived from words chosen by the user; insecure because humans are poor sources of randomness; not to be confused with wallet-generated recovery codes.

The key-stretching function BIP39 uses: 2,048 rounds of HMAC-SHA512 over the recovery words with the salt 'mnemonic'+passphrase, producing a 512-bit seed; slows brute force modestly and mainly helps when an attacker knows part of the code.
The second input to a key-stretching function that defeats precomputed lookup tables; in BIP39 it is the constant string 'mnemonic' concatenated with the optional passphrase.

A Bitcoin public key offers about 128 bits of security (roughly 2^128 elliptic-curve operations to break), which is why 128 bits of seed entropy (12 words) is considered sufficient; more only helps if part of the code leaks.

User-entered description attached to an address or transaction (e.g., 'Paid Bob for podcast'); stored only in the local wallet database, not on the blockchain; not deterministic, so not restorable from a recovery code. BIP329 proposes an export format.
Proposed standard format for exporting wallet labels so they can be backed up and used in other applications.

Backing up wallet data beyond keys (labels, exchange rates, Lightning channel state); one approach is frequent automatic backups of the whole database encrypted with a seed-derived key, which can safely sit on untrusted storage.
An offchain payment protocol increasingly supported by wallets; its channel state is nonkey data that a recovery code cannot restore.
Lightning's mechanism for recovering funds after data loss; it cannot guarantee results, and a counterparty that detects your data loss may be able to steal funds.

The sequence of child indices from the master key that identifies a key, written with slashes: m/0 (first child private key), M/0 (first child public key), m/0'/0, m/44'/0'/0'/0/2. Read right to left for ancestry.

Standardized derivation paths defined by BIPs (BIP44 m/44'/0'/0' for P2PKH, BIP49 nested P2WPKH, BIP84 m/84'/0'/0' for P2WPKH, BIP86 m/86'/0'/0' for P2TR) so users need not record paths; inflexible because wallets must scan every supported path and can't restore user-specific data.

Backing up path and script information alongside the recovery code, almost always as output script descriptors (BIPs 380-386, 389), e.g., sh(multi(2,key1,key2)) or pkh([fingerprint/44'/0'/0']xpub.../1/*); exact and extensible (can hold cosigners' keys) but more to back up.
Implicit-path standards by purpose number: 49' for nested (P2SH-wrapped) P2WPKH, 84' for native segwit P2WPKH, 86' for single-key taproot P2TR; BIP44 (44') covers legacy P2PKH.

term: Master private key / master chain code
definition: The two 256-bit halves of HMAC-SHA512(root seed): the master private key m (whose public key is M = m x G) and the master chain code c, the roots of the HD tree.
256 bits of extra entropy carried with each HD key and fed into child derivation so that knowing a child key and index is not enough to derive its siblings; the root chain code comes from the seed.

The BIP32 function combining a parent key, chain code, and 32-bit index via HMAC-SHA512 into 512 bits: the left 256 bits tweak the key to make the child key, the right 256 bits become the child chain code.
The 32-bit child number: 0 to 2^31-1 (0x00000000-0x7FFFFFFF) selects normal derivation; 2^31 to 2^32-1 (0x80000000-0xFFFFFFFF) selects hardened derivation, displayed as i' or ih meaning 2^31 + i.
A key plus its chain code ('extensible' key): the root of a branch from which children can be derived; encoded with base58check as xprv or xpub.
Private key + chain code; can derive child private keys (and from them public keys) for a whole branch; base58check prefix 'xprv'.

Public key + chain code; can derive the branch's child public keys and addresses but not spend; base58check prefix 'xpub' (version 0x0488B21E); ideal for web servers, watch-only wallets, and cold-storage receive addresses.

The maximum number of consecutive unused addresses a wallet will generate and scan past before assuming there are no later payments; when exhausted, a wallet must refuse new addresses, generate beyond the gap (risking missed funds on restore), or reuse addresses (hurting privacy).

Child derivation that feeds the parent private key (not the public key) into HMAC-SHA512, breaking the link between parent public key and child chain code so a leaked child private key plus chain code cannot expose the parent or siblings; best practice makes all level-1 children of the master hardened.
Convention that the first hardened index under the master key declares the tree's purpose (m/i'/...), so different structures are namespaced.

Multi-account HD structure with purpose 44': m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index. coin_type 0' = Bitcoin, 1' = Bitcoin testnet; change 0 = receiving, 1 = change addresses (normal derivation so xpubs can be exported).
Keeping private keys (e.g., an xprv or hardware signing device) offline while an xpub online generates receive addresses; spending requires bringing the transaction to the offline signer.
Widely used open-source merchant payment processor that generates per-order addresses from an xpub; mitigates gap-limit problems with very large gap limits and invoice rate limiting.
